classification.difficultyReason: Calculate distance at constant speed with minutes-to-hours and kilometres-to-metres conversions.

questions.mappingNote: The question directly assesses distance from speed and elapsed time.
questions.methodNote: Multiply speed by time in hours, then convert kilometres to metres, as in Example 1(b).

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate distance at constant speed with minutes-to-hours and kilometres-to-metres conversions.

classification.difficultyReason: Multiply speed by time using matching units.

questions.mappingNote: No rate conversion is required; distance calculation is the assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Distance equals constant speed multiplied by elapsed time.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Multiply speed by time using matching units.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the taught rate-unit conversions, choosing multiplication or division for distance and time units in each direction.

questions.mappingNote: All three parts directly assess conversion between rate units.
questions.methodNote: Example 1(a) converts kilometres to metres and hours to minutes and seconds in successive steps; reverse these conversions for m/s to km/h.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert speed units in both directions using distance and time conversion factors.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate average speed after converting mixed time units or both distance and time units.

questions.mappingNote: The requested average speeds require unit-consistent distance-over-time calculations.
questions.methodNote: Use average speed as distance divided by time. Example 3 converts the time to a fraction of an hour before dividing; use metres and seconds for part c.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate average speed after converting mixed time units or both distance and time units.

classification.difficultyReason: Express constant-speed travel as d=80t and identify the speed as the distance–time gradient, following the taught interpretation.

questions.mappingNote: Interpreting the gradient as constant speed is the most advanced directly assessed requirement.
questions.methodNote: Follow Example 2: generalise distances after 1 and 2 hours to d=vt, then identify the constant speed as the gradient.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Represent constant speed with a linear formula and identify speed as its gradient.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert a speed, construct a table and graph, and use the resulting linear formula.

questions.mappingNote: Question 6 applies those methods to a journey beginning at zero distance and ending at 100 km.
questions.methodNote: Example 1 converts hourly rates to minute rates; Example 4 constructs a constant-rate table and graph, then gives a formula with its physical domain.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert a speed, construct a table and graph, and use the resulting linear formula.

classification.difficultyReason: Read intercepts, calculate a decreasing rate, and model original and changed conditions.

questions.mappingNote: The supplied tank graph uses the same intercept-and-gradient model, followed by changed initial volume and outflow.
questions.methodNote: Example 4 interprets gradient as a constant volume rate and the vertical intercept as initial volume. Example 5 models a decreasing quantity with a negative gradient and bounded domain.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read intercepts, calculate a decreasing rate, and model original and changed conditions.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct and interpret a journey graph, write a formula, and compare arrival time with sunset.

questions.mappingNote: The printed distance-travelled wording supports an increasing graph, while the indicated Example 5 and answer book use distance remaining. The competing interpretations materially change parts a–c.
questions.methodNote: Examples 1–2 use distance travelled = speed × time; Example 5 instead models distance remaining with a decreasing line.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct and interpret a journey graph, write a formula, and compare arrival time with sunset.

classification.difficultyReason: Replace each stated proportionality with an equation, divide the supplied corresponding values to find its constant, and state the formula.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts assess determining a direct-proportion equation from one corresponding pair. The supplied reuse candidates have different complete tasks and are inapplicable.
questions.methodNote: Page 7 defines direct proportion using y = kx and Example 6 demonstrates substituting a corresponding pair to find k before stating the formula. Page 11 repeats the direct-proportion summary.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find a direct-proportion constant from one supplied pair, then state the formula.

classification.difficultyReason: Transform the independent variable, graph the transformed data and use its gradient to identify a quadratic variation model.

questions.mappingNote: Question 2 directly applies the change-of-variable table and graph method to x², then uses the transformed graph's gradient to obtain y=2x². Variation from a table is the closest primary catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Pages 8–9 demonstrate replacing t by t² in a value table, plotting the dependent variable against the squared variable, and identifying the gradient as the constant of proportionality. Page 7 establishes the straight-line-through-origin criterion; Examples 8–9 model variation with powers.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Transform the independent variable, graph the transformed data and use its gradient to identify a quadratic variation model.

classification.difficultyReason: Plot a nonlinear relationship, transform the independent variable and identify a constant ratio.

questions.mappingNote: Question 3 applies that change-of-variable method to sqrt(p): complete its row, compare q/sqrt(p), then write q=k sqrt(p). The original q-against-p plot remains a nonlinear curve.
questions.methodNote: Pages 7–9 identify a constant of proportionality using a ratio and transform the independent variable to reveal direct proportion; examples find k by substitution before writing the formula.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Plot a nonlinear relationship, transform the independent variable and identify a constant ratio.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate direct-proportion statements into symbols, including a cube and a square root.

questions.mappingNote: All three parts assess representing a verbal direct-proportion relationship symbolically. No constant or numerical solution is requested.
questions.methodNote: Page 7 defines proportional notation; pages 8–9 extend it to powers through change of variable; page 10 explicitly models proportionality to a cube.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate direct-proportion statements into symbols, including a cube and a square root.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate direct-proportion notation into words, retaining the specified powers and square root.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts ask for verbal interpretations rather than finding a constant or solving an equation. Describe and represent direct variation is the closest catalogue skill; retain the powers and square root in the verbal descriptions.
questions.methodNote: Page 7 explicitly translates direct proportionality into the symbol ∝. Pages 8–9 explain direct proportion to a square; page 10 uses direct proportion to a cube.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate direct-proportion notation into words, retaining the specified powers and square root.

classification.difficultyReason: Determine each variation constant, then substitute forwards or rearrange backwards; the hardest step isolates n squared and takes its positive square root for an exact answer.

questions.mappingNote: Part a follows Example 7's constant-first method. Part b applies the square-variation method of Example 8, including its positive-root convention. The most advanced directly assessed skill is modelling direct variation with a power.
questions.methodNote: Write the proportionality equation with constant k, substitute the supplied pair to determine k, then substitute or rearrange for the requested variable. Example 7 models linear variation; Example 8 models square variation and taking the positive square root. Exercise 18B specifies positive variables.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Determine proportionality constants, substitute values and recover a positive variable from its square, retaining exact answers.

classification.difficultyReason: Determine constants of proportionality and formulas for linear, square-root and cubic relationships.

questions.mappingNote: Part a follows Examples 6–7 for linear proportionality. Part b applies the same constant-finding method to the square-root expression. Part c follows Example 9's cubic model. The power-model skill covers the most advanced directly assessed relationship.
questions.methodNote: Replace proportionality with an equation containing k, substitute the given pair, solve for k and state the resulting formula.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Determine constants of proportionality and formulas for linear, square-root and cubic relationships.

classification.difficultyReason: Select a complete nonzero table pair to determine k, then use multiplication or division according to which variable is missing.

questions.mappingNote: The question supplies direct-variation tables and asks for their constants and missing entries, matching variation-from-table. No supplied reuse candidate has the same complete task.
questions.methodNote: Use y=kx, substitute a supplied nonzero pair to find k, then substitute into the resulting equation to find either variable. Page 7 defines the constant as y/x; Examples 6 and 7 demonstrate finding k and substituting in both directions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find a constant ratio from a supplied pair and use direct proportion to complete each value table.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret the map scale as a constant rate and scale the known actual distance to the requested map distance.

questions.mappingNote: The map scale supplies one pair of directly proportional distances; calculating another distance directly assesses solving a variation equation.
questions.methodNote: Write the direct-proportion equation, substitute the known pair to find the constant, then substitute the required input, as in Examples 6 and 7. Exercise 18B specifies positive variables.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find a constant of direct proportion from a map scale and use it to calculate an actual distance.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the stated direct relationship to obtain cost per unit area, then reverse the relationship to find area from the new cost.

questions.mappingNote: The question uses the same linear direct-proportion model as the carpet-cost example, with area as the independent variable and cost supplied to determine area.
questions.methodNote: Examples 6 and 7 write the direct-proportion equation, substitute the given pair to find the constant, then substitute the new value and solve. Exercise 18B specifies positive variables.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find a direct-proportion constant from cost and area, then solve for the area at another cost.

classification.difficultyReason: Scale mass in the same ratio as beam length and round the resulting mass to the nearest kilogram.

questions.mappingNote: The mass is directly proportional to length with exponent one, so solve-variation-equation is the closest directly assessed skill. The printed Example 8 reference is retained.
questions.methodNote: Write the proportionality as an equation with constant k, substitute the given pair, determine k, and substitute the requested value. Examples 6–8 demonstrate this sequence. Exercise 18B specifies positive variables.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find a direct proportionality constant from one given pair, substitute a new length and round the resulting mass.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate the stated cubic relationship into a model, calibrate it with the known speed and power, and evaluate it at the new speed before rounding.

questions.mappingNote: This question directly assesses forming and evaluating a cubic direct-variation model, matching model-direct-variation-power.
questions.methodNote: Example 9 on page 10 models cubic variation by writing the dependent quantity as k times the cube of the independent quantity, substituting the known pair, finding k and using the resulting formula. Page 11 specifies positive variables throughout Exercise 18B.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Model cubic direct variation, determine its constant and calculate a new power with specified rounding.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the stated square law to the changed time, either finding the constant first or recognising that doubling time quadruples distance.

questions.mappingNote: The task models distance as directly proportional to the square of time and evaluates the model at a new positive time. Exercise 18B restricts variables to positive values.
questions.methodNote: Write the square-variation equation, substitute the known pair, retain the exact constant and substitute the new time. Example 10 also explains that multiplying the independent variable multiplies the dependent variable by the corresponding power.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply square variation to a change in time in a falling-object context.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply a squared scale factor to determine the effect of changing the independent variable.

questions.mappingNote: All three parts assess multiplicative changes in a direct power-variation relationship with exponent 2.
questions.methodNote: Write y=kx² and compare the value at x=1 with the value after the specified change, following the choose-one method in Example 10 on page 10. Exercise 18B specifies positive variables on page 11.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply a squared scale factor to determine the effect of changing the independent variable.

classification.difficultyReason: Determine scale factors in square variation, including recovering a radius factor using a positive square root.

questions.mappingNote: Part a applies square variation to a doubled radius; part b reverses square variation to determine the exact positive radius multiplier.
questions.methodNote: Write the proportional relationship as an equation with constant k. Example 10 chooses an initial variable value of 1 to compare changes; Examples 8 and 11 demonstrate recovering a variable using a positive root. Exercise 18B specifies positive variables.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Determine scale factors in square variation, including recovering a radius factor using a positive square root.

classification.difficultyReason: Determine multiplicative changes in a fourth-power relationship, including reversing the relationship using positive fourth roots.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts assess multiplicative changes under fourth-power direct variation; parts c and d reverse the relationship.
questions.methodNote: Write m=kn^4. Follow Example 10 by choosing an initial independent-variable value of 1 and comparing the resulting multiples of k. For reverse changes, solve the power equation using the positive root, consistent with Examples 8–9 and the exercise-wide positive-variable instruction on page 11.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Determine multiplicative changes in a fourth-power relationship, including reversing the relationship using positive fourth roots.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert each percentage change in b into a multiplier, take its square root, and interpret the resulting multiplier as a percentage increase or decrease in a.

questions.mappingNote: Question 17 directly applies Example 11's percentage-change method to square-root variation. Neither supplied reuse question has the same stem, givens or response requirements.
questions.methodNote: Example 11 writes the square-root variation equation, chooses an initial independent-variable value of 1, applies the percentage change and compares the new dependent value with its original value. Exercise 18B specifies positive variables.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert percentage changes into multipliers, apply square-root variation and interpret the resulting percentage change.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate percentage changes into factors and choose cube roots for changes from q to p but cubes for changes from p to q, then interpret the resulting percentage changes.

questions.mappingNote: The question extends the taught percentage-change method to cube-root variation and its rearranged cubic relationship; both directions are directly assessed.
questions.methodNote: Examples 10 and 11 choose an original variable value of 1, apply the change factor, and compare the resulting quantities. Example 11 rearranges the variation equation when the other variable is requested. Exercise 18B specifies positive variables.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate percentage effects in both directions for a cube-root variation relationship.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert the mixed duration into hours, multiply by the walking speed, and convert the resulting kilometres into metres.

questions.mappingNote: Andrew's walking question uses the same distance calculation and unit conversions as Example 1(b), with a mixed hours-and-minutes duration.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 obtains distance by multiplying constant speed by elapsed time. Page 3, Example 1(b), converts minutes to hours before multiplying by speed, then converts kilometres to metres.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert mixed hours and minutes to hours, calculate distance at a constant speed and convert kilometres to metres.

classification.difficultyReason: Multiply speed by time using already compatible units.

questions.mappingNote: Question 2 directly applies distance = speed × time. Metres per second and seconds are compatible, so no conversion is required.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 develops distance as constant speed multiplied by elapsed time. Page 3, Example 1(b), substitutes speed and time to calculate distance, converting units where necessary.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Multiply speed by time using already compatible units.

classification.difficultyReason: Two direct speed conversions using metres per kilometre and seconds per hour.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts directly assess conversion between speed units; convert-rate-units is the supplied catalogue match.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 interprets rates per unit time. Page 3, Example 1(a), converts kilometres to metres, then divides by 60 for each conversion from per hour to per minute and from per minute to per second. Reverse those operations for conversion to kilometres per hour.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Two direct speed conversions using metres per kilometre and seconds per hour.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert hours and minutes to a single duration in hours, then divide each distance by that duration to obtain average speed.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts directly apply Example 3's method to a duration of 1 hour 20 minutes, giving average speeds in kilometres per hour.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 defines average speed as distance travelled divided by time taken. Page 4, Example 3, converts hours and minutes to an exact fractional number of hours, then divides distance by that fraction using its reciprocal.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert a mixed hours-and-minutes duration to hours and divide distance by time.

classification.difficultyReason: Express distance at a constant speed as a formula and identify the speed as the graph's gradient.

questions.mappingNote: Question 5 applies the same formula-and-gradient method with speed 95 km/h; constant-rate-graphs is the most advanced directly assessed supplied skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 models constant-speed distance by d=60t and identifies the gradient as speed. Page 3, Example 2, derives d=100t from a constant speed of 100 km/h and identifies the gradient as 100.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Express distance at a constant speed as a formula and identify the speed as the graph's gradient.

classification.difficultyReason: Determine constants of proportionality for linear and square variation, then calculate exact values.

questions.mappingNote: Part (a) uses p=kq to find p and q. Part (b) uses a=kb², determines the formula and substitutes two values of b. Square-variation modelling is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 7 defines direct proportion using a constant k and Example 6 finds k by substituting a given pair. Page 8 Example 7 substitutes into the resulting equation to find either variable. Page 9 Example 8 applies the same procedure to square variation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Determine constants of proportionality for linear and square variation, then calculate exact values.

classification.difficultyReason: Read a complete nonzero pair from each table to find y/x, then apply that constant to the supplied x-values.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts apply this method to paired table values: (1,12) gives k=12 in part a, and (2,3) gives k=3/2 in part b.
questions.methodNote: Page 7 defines direct proportionality as y=kx and identifies k from one nonzero pair. Examples 6 and 7 substitute the supplied pair to find k, then use the resulting formula to calculate further values.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use one given nonzero pair to find the constant of direct proportionality and complete each table.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply cubic direct variation to determine the multiplicative effect of changing the independent variable.

questions.mappingNote: All three parts use precisely the cubic scaling method of Example 10, with factors 2, 3 and 1/4. The power-variation skill is the closest supplied classification.
questions.methodNote: Page 10, Example 10, writes cubic proportionality as a constant times the cube, chooses an initial independent-variable value of 1, and compares the resulting values after scaling. Page 11 reinforces modelling proportionality with a constant.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply cubic direct variation to determine the multiplicative effect of changing the independent variable.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine two different variation models with independent constants, use the two equal-output conditions to construct simultaneous equations, and solve them to obtain one expression.

questions.mappingNote: The question combines a quantity proportional to x with a quantity proportional to 1/x². Its two conditions require simultaneous equations, beyond the single-constant worked examples supplied.
questions.methodNote: Pages 7–11 introduce constants of proportionality, substitution to determine a constant, and variation involving powers. The supplied teaching does not demonstrate determining two variation constants simultaneously.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine two variation models and use two conditions to determine both constants simultaneously.

classification.difficultyReason: Form a direct-variation equation involving two expressions, determine its constant, then factorise a quadratic and select the positive solution.

questions.mappingNote: The question applies the taught constant-of-proportionality method to x²+y² and x+y. Its most advanced directly assessed step is factorising the resulting quadratic and rejecting the negative root. Original teaching evidence for that prerequisite remains missing.
questions.methodNote: Page 7 defines direct proportion using a constant and Example 6 determines that constant by substitution. Examples 7–9 reinforce substitution and solving the resulting equation; Example 8 selects a positive square root. These pages do not demonstrate solving a quadratic with both linear and squared terms by factorisation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Form a direct-variation equation involving two expressions, determine its constant, then factorise a quadratic and select the positive solution.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose to square the proportionality equation, expand and regroup to expose a constant ratio between a squared plus b squared and ab, and justify excluding degenerate constant values.

questions.mappingNote: Special products is the most advanced directly assessed skill: both binomial squares must be expanded and rearranged to exhibit a constant multiple of ab. Original teaching evidence for this algebraic prerequisite is missing.
questions.methodNote: Page 7 defines direct proportionality using a nonzero constant and Examples 6–11 replace proportionality by an equation. None of the inspected teaching pages demonstrates the required special-product proof manipulation. The teacher answer supplies the intended square-expand-rearrange proof but is answer evidence only.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Introduce a constant of proportionality, expand two squares and rearrange a symbolic identity to prove another proportional relationship.

classification.difficultyReason: Account for a delayed departure and determine when two constant-speed journeys reach the same position.

questions.mappingNote: The task directly assesses speed, distance and elapsed time with different departure times. The equation-based solution is mathematically verified, but its overtaking-method prerequisite lacks supplied original teaching evidence.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 develops distance as speed multiplied by time; page 3 demonstrates time-unit conversion and constant-speed distance formulas; page 4 demonstrates exact fractional-hour calculations. These inspected examples do not demonstrate delayed-start overtaking or equating two journey distances.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Account for a delayed departure and determine when two constant-speed journeys reach the same position.

classification.difficultyReason: Read a piecewise distance–time graph, calculate segment speeds and interpret distance remaining and clock time.

questions.mappingNote: Read distances at specified times, subtract endpoint distances for each hour, and divide by elapsed time to obtain segment speeds. For distance remaining, subtract from the supplied 200 km total and read the first corresponding graph time.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 relates distance–time gradient to speed. Page 3 defines average speed as distance travelled divided by time taken. Page 4 Example 3 substitutes distance and elapsed time into that formula.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read a piecewise distance–time graph, calculate segment speeds and interpret distance remaining and clock time.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine opposite-direction travel, an exact time conversion and a fractional relationship between two speeds.

questions.mappingNote: Calculating the two average speeds is the principal assessed task; the fractional speed relationship supplies the second condition. The opposite-direction modelling step requires additional original taught-method evidence.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 relates distance to constant speed and time. Example 1 on page 3 converts minutes to hours before multiplying speed by time. Example 3 on page 4 calculates average speed using distance divided by time. These pages do not demonstrate opposite-direction separation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine opposite-direction travel, an exact time conversion and a fractional relationship between two speeds.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret both plotted journeys and their speeds, then obtain an exact meeting time by using a common time origin, accounting for Albert's delayed departure, and equating distances from town A.

questions.mappingNote: The whole question chiefly interprets a supplied distance–time graph. Parts b and c calculate segment speeds; part d additionally requires an exact intersection calculation whose taught-method evidence is missing from the supplied context.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 relates constant speed to distance–time gradient. Page 3 demonstrates distance divided by time and distance formulas. Page 5 Example 5 models distance remaining using a negative gradient and a nonzero intercept. These support parts a–c and the individual journey formulas, but do not demonstrate equating two journeys with different departure times.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Interpret two journeys with different departure times and determine their exact meeting time.
